During the Seven Years' War it was put to military use as the forerunner of the bugle. At the end of the eighteenth century horns were given tone holes and keys, and around 1800 keyed horns appeared in Dublin and London and entered British and European military music and brass bands. After the piston valve was invented in the 1820s, Heinrich Stölzel of Berlin sold a valved horn in 1828; in Bavaria it was called the Flügelhorn and replaced the keyed horn as the high melodic instrument. Adolphe Sax was also inspired by the valved horn when he developed the saxhorn. In the late 1890s Johannes Kuhlo and his father Eduard Kuhlo brought brass ensemble playing into the German Protestant church and developed the rotary-valve kuhlohorn. From the middle of the twentieth century the flugelhorn entered jazz soloing and pop music, and it also appears in East European and Dutch military bands, usually played by trumpeters doubling.

The flugelhorn (H-S 423.232) is a treble brass instrument developed in Europe / Germany, of the lip-reed aerophones, the horn and brass family. It looks like the trumpet and the cornet but has a wider bore that flares conically, is mostly in B flat, and has three piston valves; rotary valves are also found in central and eastern Europe. The mouthpiece is deeper and funnel-shaped, the fingering is the same as the trumpet's, and it is usually played by trumpeters doubling. It comes early from horns and bugles, used in hunting, military music and brass bands; later it also appears in jazz, pop, British brass bands, Dutch and Belgian military bands and orchestral works.
